If I speak along the lines I speak to-night, I will make an open confession-it is said confession is sometimes good for the soul-that it is greatly due to the lessons which the hon. member taught me. He will remember quite well that for years we sat in this House as desk-mates. He said, upon several occasions since this session began, that he was the father of free trade in this House. Perhaps I will not go quite as far as that.
If the hon. member will pardon me, I never used that expression about myself. I never called myself the father of anybody except four boys.
The teacher?

I never describe myself.
Mr. DEVLiN: Does the hon. gentleman say that he was not a teacher? Why, the hon. gentleman pointed out to me on a hundred and one occasions-and this is no breach of confidence-that I must be blind if I could not see that free trade was the only thing to save this country.
Does not the hon. gentleman remember how cleverly he put the matter when he spoke of the rays of the sun coming through the window, and turning to me, said:
" Would you put a wall in front of those rays?" Does not the hon. gentleman remember that language? " Why," he said, "it is the same thing exactly when you try to build up a wall against the free entry of goods into this country." Now, I take it that my hon. friend was sincere when he said that; I may be credulous, but I certainly thought he was sincere. And when I heard him say this afternoon that this was not an opportune time for a resolution such as this, I began to think: Has my old desk-mate gone back on the principles which actuated him during so many years, simply because he has changed from a seat upon this side of the House to a seat upon that? We all have the privilege of changing our opinions, of course, and I hope that none of us is so glued to any one particular opinion in non-essentials that he will not change it on any account. But the hon. member for Red Deer has pointed out, not on one or two or three or half-a-dozen occasions in this House, but in season and

out of season, that free trade as they have it in England is the proper thing for this country. Remembering how he had told us with that eloquence of his how he had learned free trade under William Ewart Gladstone, we thought he was going to instil into the minds not only of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House but of hon. gentlemen opposite, the same undying principle^ -until this afternoon, when he said: "A punctilio, the merest technicality, prevents me from supporting the opinions I have held on the tariff during my whole political career."
Mr. Speaker, what is good for this country in the matter of trade? Is a low or a high tariff the best? The Acting Prime Minister will tell me that a high tariff is best; my hon. friend from Red Deer, that a low tariff is best. The hon. gentleman from Red Deer says that a low tariff is best, provided there are no technicalities in the way. Away with such talk about technicalities! How often have I heard the hon. member from Red Deer use similar language: Away with your technicalities and your precedents; give us free trade.
I must now leave, with very great regret, my hon. friend from Red Deer and turn to my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Levi Thomson) for a very brief moment. He is another gentleman who sat with us upon this side of the House; another gentleman who said that he had great difficulty in finding converts, as he put it, to the resolution which I have now in my hand, proposed on the 29th of May, 1917, by the Hon. Frank Oliver, when the war was perhaps at its most critical stage. The hon. member says that hp is thoroughly in accord with this present amendment, I understand that the hon. member is a lawyer, who occasionally does some farming. He wants the West to know that he is in favour of this resolution, and h<e is going to support it by voting against it. He hopes the Government will give consideration to the matter. Why, my hon. friend must know that all Governments give consideration to all matters that come btefore them; oftentimes that consideration is unfavourable, and sometimes it is favourable, and judging by the attitude of those on the Government benches this afternoon and their attitude during the past few days I do not think I am prophesying rashly when I tell the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that the Government is giving very serious consideration to this question, and its final decision will be unfavourable. After saying that he is in favour of the resolution, the hon. member goes on to say
that he cannot support it because it might result in the defeat of the Government. Surely the hon. gentleman h-as not reached the stage where he clings more strongly to Government than to principle. I can hardly believe the hon. gentleman is sincere, because upon other occasions when he sat upon this side of the House looking across at the Government he did not care whether the Government was defeated or sustained. |He believed then in principle, but now he has apparently changed, not his principles, let me hope, but his mind. A strong argument which the hon. member brought to the debate this afternoon, and which must have appealed to you, Mr. Speaker, was that whilst he wanted to support the resolution by voting against it, he could not vote for it because it would place his western colleagues in a falsie position. Mr. Speaker, his vote will not place his western colleagues in a false position if I know anything of the sentiments of the West as we rtead of them in the Unionist press of today. The West is demanding a lower tariff. Is that not so? The West is not asking hon. members representing western constituencies to wait, but is dtemanding immediate action. Am I right, or wrong? The hon. member, however, says that he does not want to vote for this resolution, because it will placte the western members in a false light. And that can be readily understood. Western Canada has sent representatives here in great numbers to support a lower tariff, and is now demanding action. The West says to its representatives: Now is your time to ask for a lower tariff; we want you to act immediately. One h<m. member from the West replies:	Will you
not wait until the Budget comes down? Another hon. member says: Will you not . wait until we see what consideration the Government gives the matter? And yet another hon. gentleman tells us that he will go back to the West and explain his position. He says: It would have been all right for me to do it, but I would have placed my western colleagues in a false light. It seems to me, Sir, that we have come to a time in the political history of Canada when the representatives of the people must not be actuated by political motives, but solely by motives of principle. We, unfortunately-and I shall only allude to the fact in passing-have lost our leader. We have lost one in whom we could confidently place even our own judgment. We were so sure of the greatness of his mind, ve were so sure of the position he would take, and that his every action would conduce to the greater advantage of Canada, that we

could safely follow Mm On all political questions which might come before this House. We no longer have him with us, but we have the beautiful fruits of his life work, the principles which he laid down and which should guide not only the Liberals who supported him, but every man who is intent on his country's good and wishes to do his duty by those who sent him here and by the Dominion at large-not as he sees it in his own parochial way but' from the broader standpoint of the whole Dominion. Sir, these principles have been instilled into the minds of Liberals in this House and throughout the Dominion, including my Liberal friends on the other side of the House who would follow them if they had the courage of their convictions. I listened with much interest to my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster), who gave a good reason why his motion should be adopted-indeed, he gave many good reasons. He took the question up in its economic phase, and although I shall not weary the House by repeating the virtues of the resolution, I will assure my hon. friends from the West that in supporting the resolution we are not at all guided by what action they may take. We do not care a jot whether they desire to place their colleagues in a false or a fair light in the House. That is a matter of their own concern. But what we wish to place upon the record is the fact that, of all classes in this Dominion, the one class that is not protected is the farming population; and we wish further to record our recognition of the just demands of the farmers and our support of them in those demands. Will technicalities stand in the way? Let that same resolution in a different form be introduced by any hon. gentleman on the opposite side as a Government measure, and I appeal to my leader to tell me whether I am right in saying that hon. members on this side would give the same measure of support to the resolution so introduced as they propose to give to that now before the House.
It is not my intention to endeavour to embarrass the Government. Heaven knows, Sir, they are sufficiently embarrassed as it stands, although they have brought this embarrassment on themselves. They have made innumerable pledges, and if they cannot fulfil those pledges, well, we can only shrug our shoulders and pray for them. But I want to say one word to my friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. T. A. Crerar). We recognize the extremely difficult position he is in, and sympathize with him. We under-
	i
stand that he has been for many years the spokesman for the farming communities in the West. He entered this Government as a matter of conscience, he tells us, and adds that to support this resolution would place him in a false light, it would perhaps mean the defeat of the Government; in any even he did not think the present was an opportune time to propose it. Well, I readily agree with the hon. minister in that last argument; any resolution which may have a tendency to embarrass a Government is likely to be regarded by that Government as inopportune at any time, war or no war. The resolution which was proposed on the 29th of May, 1917, and which was supported by the hon. gentlemen now seated on the other side of the House, was not, according to my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, introduced at an opportune time. Its introduction, I take it, would be eminently opportune if the Hon. the Minister of Agriculture happened to be seated on this side of the House; but he is not on this side, hence his opinion. Other members following him spoke along the same lines. Well, Mr. Speaker, any time is an opportune time for the farmers of the East; and if it is not an opportune time for the farmers of the West, my advice to hon. gentlemen representing Western interests will be to wait until such time presents itself. If the farmers of the West are satisfied to wait indefinitely, it is well; but we who represent constitutencies wherein farmers are to be found, and who know something about the farming communities of Eastern Canada, are of opinion that the farmers are not prepared to wait any longer for action on the part of the Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. F. B. CARVELL (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, considering the importance of the amendment before the House, and the number of times that I have discussed the tariff question in this House during the last fourteen or fifteen years, I do not feel justified in giving a silent vote upon the amendment, and for that reason I shall proceed to place myself on record very briefly as to my position. In doing so I hope it will be distinctly understood that I am speaking for nobody but myself; I am not attempting to represent the Government, and I am speaking, in so far as it is possible to do so, as an ordinary member of the House. Like my friend from Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. :Levi Thomson) when I heard the amendment read this afternoon it sounded very familiar to me: it was practically the Oliver resolution of 1917, which

I seconded, which I supported, which I honestly believed in when I supported it, and with the principles of which I am strongly in accord to-night. There are two matters referred to in the amendment now before us which were not included in the Oliver resolution. The first is a declaration that the Reciprocity Agreement of 1911 should be brought into force by the Parliament of Canada at the present time in order that we might have the advantages of it.
Let me say, Sir, that there was no man in Canada who honestly believed in the virtues of the Reciprocity Agreement of 1911 to a greater extent than I did. There has never been anything in my whole political experience which I viewed so favourably from the economic standpoint-which I believed would be to the advantage of the great majority of the people of Canada-as I did the Reciprocity Agreement. I have not changed my mind one jot or tittle down to the present day, and the greatest regret of my life-not from any personal feelings, but from the standpoint of the public-was that the Reciprocity Agreement of 1911 was not sustained by the people at the polls. 1 am, however, unable to agree with my friend that any very great good would come by the adoption of the Reciprocity Agreement by this Parliament at the present time, for the simple reason that practically everything which the Reciprocity Agreement grants to the people of Canada has already been obtained, either by the action of the United States Congress, or by the action of the Canadian Government during the last three or four years. Lumber has been made free. That means a tremendous amount to the eastern portions of Canada, and I believe to some extent as well to the western portions of the Dominion. Fresh fish have been made free, which must be a tremendous gain, I know it is in fact, to the people of Eastern Canada. A great proportion of the agricultural products of Canada are free into the United States. Cement has been made free, boots and shoes are free; and practically, as I said before, everything which is produced in large quantities, and which means a great deal to the industries and the producers of Canada, now goes into the United States free of duty. There are, it is true, a great many small items, referred to by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) this afternoon, which are not free, but they play a very small part in the general trade of the country.
In addition to the articles which have been made free by the United States Congress, wheat and wheat products, or the
great majority of them, have been made free by the action of this Government. The same thing can be said of potatoes, due, of course, to taking advantage of the provisions of the recent United States tariff. My reason for saying that the adoption of this policy would not be of very much value to Canada at the present time is, that I always contended that the reciprocity arrangement was not a treaty, but was simply an agreement by which like tariffs should be adopted by the two countries on a certain list of articles. It is well known that a change has taken place in the political complexion of the Congress of the United States during the past three or four months. What course the new Congress may take I do not know; but I am sure that any action which this Government or this Parliament may take to-night would have no influence whatever upon the action which the United States Congress may take when it meets, some time probably in the month of May.
I am not going to-night over all the ancient history in regard to this question, but I do feel that I ought to read one extract from the letter written by the two gentlemen who negotiated the treaty on the part of Canada in 1911, to show that this was not a treaty, but simply an agreement that certain tariff reciprocal arrangements should be provided by the two countries. I am going to take the liberty of doing that because it seems to me it goes to the very pith, the very heart, of the proposal of my hon. friend as embodied in the amendment which he has submitted. I am reading now from the letter, dated 21st January, 1911, signed by W. S. Fielding and William Paterson, in accepting the proposal of the United States Government as contained in a memorandum of the American Secretary of State to them. I will read one paragraph from that letter, to show what was the real intention of the document. It is to be found at page 2457 of Hansard, 1911:
Nevertheless, It is distinctly understood that we do not attempt to bind for the future the action of the United States Congress or the Parliament of Canada, but that each of these authorities shall be absolutely free to make any change of tariff policy or of any other matter covered by the present arrangement, that may be deemed expedient.
With that understanding, and with the changed conditions that have taken place in the United States, I can see no very great good in the Parliament of Canada, after nearly eight years have gone by, attempting to adopt the provisions of that agreement, and therefore I have no hesita-

tion whatever in voting against that portion of my hon. friend's amendment.
The hon. gentleman next deals with the repeal of the Customs War Tax imposed in 1915. I want to say here that I realize the full gravity of the statement which I am making, or about to make. I was opposed to the imposition of these duties in 1915; I did not believe they were necessary for the purpose for which they were intended. While it is true they may have brought in some revenue, I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that they have added a tremendous burden on the consumers of Canada. I was opposed to them then, and I have failed yet to be convinced that they were necessary.
As to the remainder of the amendment, it is practically the Oliver resolution of 1917, to which I have referred before, and I have but very little quarrel with any of the sentiments expressed in it. I agreed with it in 1917, and I have not seen very much to cause me to change my opinion at the present time.
I do, however, want to point out to my hon. friends opposite that, as was said by the hon. membeT from Prince, P.B.I. (Mr. Read), a man has a right to change. his mind if he finds that he is wrong. If a man has any honesty about him, and is convinced that he is wrong in his views, he will not hesitate to change them. I have not arrived at that point yet, but I may tell my hon. friends frankly that I am very much at sea as to what should be the policy of this country during the next three or four years, as to the whole question of the taxation by which we are going to raise a revenue. Earlier in this session I took occasion to point out, in a very brief manner, and in a very general way, the financial situation as I viewed it in Canada. I pointed out that I could not see how, under present conditions, we were going to raise the last $100,000,000 of revenue required in the next twelve months, after the current fiscal year, and I have listened in vain for any person on either side of the House even to discuss the matter, let alone point to the solution.
I think I can go as far as to say that I have seen no very great change in the attitude of the people of Canada and their representatives in their demand for the expenditure of public monies. I am afraid that my teaching has not produced very much result up to date. On account of the changed financial conditions, I tell you very frankly that I am at sea to know exactly what ought to be the proper method of

raising taxation in this country. I think practically every method' which we have ever heard of before and which we can conceive of in the future is going to be necessary in order to produce the required amount of money; and I want to point out to my friends opposite that the debt of this country will ue a billion dollars more before the affairs of the present year are wound up than it was when the Oliver amendment was discussed. While that may seem a very unimportant matter to some hon. gentlemen of this House and some people in this country, it is a very, very serious matter to me.
With many of the general principles laid down by this amendment I am in hearty accord. I do not believe in the doctrine of protection for protection's sake. I do not believe that any industry is entitled to protection to such an extent that it means the prohibition of the importation into this country of the article covered by that industry. I do believe that the raw material of the farmer, his agricultural implements, should be made free, or as nearly free as ft is possible to make them under existing conditions. It may be that the manufacture of some of those articles could not exist in Canada if they were made absolutely free. I have not been convinced of that yet, but I am willing to listen to argument, and I would feel like deciding only after a very mature consideration of the subject. But I believe that a great majority of the agricultural implements of this country ought to be free to the farmers.
Now, I realize, Mr. Speaker, that I am making statements which, considering my position, mean a good deal to me. I can only say that when I entered this Government-I am not going over the very, very long and somewhat unpleasant conditions which existed between the month of April and the month of October, 1917; possibly another occasion may arise when they can be discussed-I did so after the most mature deliberation, which many of my good old friends opposite know all about, and nobody knows so well as does my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding). II did so for one specific purpose and for a specified time. The purpose, I am happy to say, has been achieved; the time has not yet expired. During the election in the province of New Brunswick I issued a letter to my constituents and to the people of our province, setting forth the fact that the Government was to be composed of an equal number of former Conservatives and former Liberals, for the

purpose of carrying on the war and providing recruits for our army, and that it would continue for the duration of the war
and a reasonable time thereafter for demobilization.
Demobilization has not yet been completed, and so far as I am concerned my contract has not expired. Therefore, regardless of what may have been my opinions in 1917, and regardless of 10 p.m. what my opinions may be today, on economic questions I am not going to take any action which would put this Government out of power while the soldiers are on the ocean coming back and before they are demobilized, and which action would probably, if carried out to its logical conclusion, bring on a general election while this great movement is in process.
I have no fault to find with my hon. friends for bringing up the motion as they have done; that is their business. I have been in this House long enough I think to know the political game pretty well, I have supported governments and I have been in opposition, and I realize the situation. If my friends wish to bring this up at this particular time, it is not according to my views of good political strategy, but, that is their affair, and I realize they are not asking my advice, and I am not tendering it. But the motion having been brought up I am perfectly prepared to face the situation, and I do not think there will be any question that everybody on this side of the House will be prepared to take the same stand exactly, and to vote upon this matter simply for the reason I think very largely that it would be little short of a crime to bring on a general election in Canada under present conditions.
It is all very well for my friends to say, "Well, accept the amendment." Let us get down to earth for a moment. I tell my friends, and they know very well, that this Government could not accept it, and when they say, "Accept it," they are simply asking this Government to do something which is impossible; it could not be done. Therefore it means a vote, and a vote which, if the amendment carried, would mean the resignation of the Government and a general election. I am not prepared to take that responsibility to-night, the members on this side are not taking that responsibility. Further, I do not believe there are more than two or three on the other side who would assume such a responsibility if they knew that was going to be the result.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have stated my views, perhaps somewhat frankly, and I propose to stand by this Government until the soldiers are home. When that time arrives it will be up to me, the same as it will be to every other man in this country, to do exactly what he has a mind to do. I am making no promises of what I will do; I believe that sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof, and when that time .arrives I am absolutely free to take any course which I consider in the interests of the country and in honour to myself.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac): Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in support of the resolution. We in this country with abundant resources have struggled against the tide of protection for more than forty years, and we have fought a losing fight. Protection was inaugurated about forty years ago, and since that time we have been losing in population at the rate of two hundred thousand people per annum. Instead of having as we should havo had fifteen million people in the Dominion, at the last census we had only about seven million. That was largely due to the protective tariff, which induced the people to go into the cities, the manufacturing centres, at the expense of the rural districts.
When the Liberal Administration came into power in 1896 and advocated their low tariff policy, they at the same time inaugurated a system of immigration, and they were able to get a very much larger number of immigrants from the British Isles and from the United States than had ever been attracted to this country before. We gained in population from 1901 to 1911 1,835,000 people and in the preceding ten years we gained only 530,000 people. During the 1901-11 period we gained that number of people largely from the British Isles and the United States, and they were mainly people coming to settle on the land. But again in 1911 and after that period our immigration fell off and our people quit settling on the land to any extent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there has been a good deal of talk in this country by the protectionists for some time past about the production of wealth. Well, the production of wealth in this country comes largely from the land.
The wealth of the nation is created for us in our magnificent land, timber, fishery, and mineral resources, but the only producer of wealth is labour. If you exhaust the timber resources and do not replace

them by reforestation; if you deplete the minerals or the fisheries, you are drawing on capital account; but agricultural production is practically self perpetuating if it is properly carried on. The soil, therefore, is the place from which we should largely draw our wealth. For* the last forty years the protected manufacturer has been advocating through the press, through active politicians, and on the stump, the principle that we should build up large manufacturing industries, that we should build up an export trade in manufactured goods. Well, previous to the war, England, the chief exporting country of the world, was an importer of foodstuffs. The foreign trade of England previous to the war amounted to $100 per capita; of Germany, the next greatest trading nation, $50 per capita; of the United States, only $30 per capita; and of the smaller nations lesser amounts. No nation ever built up its export business until it became an importer of foodstuffs. Great Britain before the war was importing practically two-thirds of her foodstuffs and Germany one-third; they were doing a world trade in manufactured goods. The export and import trade of the United States was largely in luxuries and in goods they did not produce; it amounted to about ten per cent of their internal trade previous to the war. The export and import business of Germany was done through a free port; the export and import business of Great Britain was done, of course, through a free trade country. It is impossible to build up an export and import business unless you do it in a free trade country or through a free port.
We are asked by the manufacturers to give them protection on their goods, to pay them a bonus on the goods we consume, in order that they may be able to build up an export business. Then, if we allow them this protective tariff or bonus, they say that they are not able to sell their goods in foreign countries; that they cannot find a market unless we, the people of Canada, furnish the funds to foreign countries with which to buy the goods which we produce in Canada. Of course they cannot sell their goods, because they cannot exchange them. The export and import business of a nation is an exchange business. If you are not able to buy from the nation to which you wish to sell, necessarily you cannot sell to that nation. They cannot ship you gold to pay for their purchase. There is not enough gold to go round; they must exchange goods with you.
Thle Bill that is to be brought down to provide for a loan to foreign countries to

enable them to buy our products provides, I understand, that two-thirds shall apply to manufactured goods and one-third to raw and finished farm products. We expect to sell, say, to Roumania and to Serbia not wheat or beef, but finished articles such as bacon, flour and other manufactured foodstuffs. That being the case, the Canadian manufacturer gets the benefit. We are being asked to furnish thte money to buy the goods of the manufacturer.
, I am not familiar enough with the rules of the House or the rules of the game of thte manufacturer to be in a position to say when this subject should be taken up and debated, but I am quite sure that so far as we are concerned, and so far as thle men who believte in a lower tariff or free trade are concerned, the time is now. Certainly the manufacturer will never be ready to say that thle time is now; and if we do not take action now, when are we to take action? The western people are asking that action be taken now, the farmers of my constituency arte asking that action be taken now. The member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Levi Thomson) may be able to explain his attitude to his constituents; but I make this suggestion to the Government: If they have any doubt as to the seriousness of the farmers in this matter, let them hold by-elections in the constituencites of Assini-boia, North Ontario, Glengarry and Stormont, and Quebec East. If they do that, they will find out what the farmers are thinking to-day. If they will not do that, and if the member for iR'ed Deer or the member for Qu'Appelle has any doubt about the attitude of the farmers in their constituencies, I make this proposal: If either of them will resign his seat I will resign mine, and we will test public opinion on this question and find out whether the peoplte think this is a proper time to give it consideration. Hon. gentlemen opposite who believe in low tariffs and in free trade should accept this as an opportune time for action, and vote accordingly.
I must admit that I was rather taken aback this afternoon when I heard the great free trade lion from Red Deer let out a yelp at the Opposition about their attitude, and then come to heel when he heard the party whip crack. If that is the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite who are free traders, we shall never get to the point where we can agree on this question in the House. But a majority of the people favour this resolution; why do not the free traders on the other side vote for it? Members on the other side as well as on this side of the House should show the people where they

stand in this matter in order that those who sent us here as their representatives may know what to expect from us.
Is my hon. friend in favour of absolute free trade for Canada?
I am in favour of absolute free trade for Canada at the present moment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question before the House is important in one or two respects, notably in that it has to be taken, if carried, to involve a vote of want of confidence in the Government. It is not my intention to discuss many of the aspects of the matter that have been touched upon this evening, but rather to reply to some remarks made by hon. gentlemen opposite who are evidently going to vote for the amendment and who have attempted to justify their vote by all the arguments that they consider necessary to support their position.
It is an amendment to the motion for going into Supply, and it is argued by the leader of the Opposition and by most of the other hon. members who have spoken on that side of the House that it is not thereby a vote of confidence motion. It is true that during the years that I have been in this House, I have.heard this point argued a good deal, and especially has it been argued that this is not necessarily to be taken as a vote of want of confidence, if the subject matter of the amendment is not of any very great importance. There may be some force in that, but I do not think' any hon. member in this House, either on this side or on the other, could possibly say that this was anything but a want of confidence motion, when it involves an absolute and complete change in the whole of our fiscal policy at the present time. A matter so fundamentally important must certainly, if brought up in this way, if carried or rejected, be regarded as a want of confidence motion, especially when it is brought in at this time before the Budget is brought down. The amendment, as every hon. member knows, relates to the whole of our fiscal system. It is intimately concerned with all our business ramifications throughout the country, and yet the leader of the Opposition said that if it was accepted, it would not be a vote of want of confidence. I can only say that from my point of view, if an amendment of that kind were accepted at this time, when the Budget is at least a few weeks off, and when the closest study is being given to
the fiscal and trade conditions of this country, I can conceive of nothing that would so disturb, dislocate and perhaps destroy the industries of this country as to have an amendment of. this kind carried at this particular moment. The leader of the Opposition rather taunted the members of the Government and other members on this side of the House and said: Waiting, waiting, what are you waiting for? My hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) said that the time to take this action is now. The leader of the Opposition said that he was extremely impatient and that everybody on that side was satisfied that the matter should not be put off, and he appealed to the record of the Liberal party on this whole matter. May I say to my hon. friend that the record of the Liberal party on this matter is not one of rushing into violent fiscal changes at very short notice? I happened to be in this country in 1896, not taking a very keen interest in politics and certainly not taking an interest in party politics. I listened to the discussions that took place throughout the country at that time. Everybody knows that the party which my hon. friend supported then and which he is supporting now was pledged to free trade as it existed in England. At that time I happened to be engaged in farming, largely fruit growing, in the Niagara peninsula, and I will recall to my hon. friend, if he does not know it; that all the people of that district-it did not matter what their party affiliations were-were greatly disturbed as to the possibility of the promises of the then Opposition being implemented. They did not know what was going to happen, and the whole case was argued very completely before a tariff commission which came around and which comprised amongst others my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), who spoke the other night. My hon. friend from.Shelburne and Queens, as a member of the Government that had been elected in 1896, did not do what the leader of i Opposition is now getting impatient to do when urging this country to rush into this change suggested to-night, but he toured through the country and listened carefully to all the presentations made by interests affected by tariff changes of any kind. As a result, the particular industry with which I was associated at that time was left practically untouched by a Government which had been pledged to free trade. As the years went on, there came demands for tariff changes, and again the Government which was supported by



the leader of the Opposition made another tour of the country and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens was at that time a member of that commission. He came out to British Columbia where I happened to be living. I was still associated with the same kind of farming and the same kind of business, and I had the honour again of putting forward some of the arguments in reference to that particular industry and everything was given a most careful and patient consideration. And, I may say, again to our satisfaction there was practically no change in the tariff as it affected that particular industry. I put these matters before the House as showing the tremendous contrast between a party which was still in power and with which my hon. friend was still associated when it had the responsibility of advocating changes in the tariff, and the attitude assumed by those hon. gentlemen who now have no responsibility at all, except to endeavour to disturb the affiliations of those who are now forming Union Government and a Union party and to try to make ammunition on that side of the House for political purposes throughout the country.
A good deal has been said about reciprocity. The word has a familiar sound to many of us who debated the matter for many weary months in the House and throughout the country I will not discuss it except to refer to the statement made by the mover of the amendment (Mr. McMaster) this afternoon, that the only thing that affected the people of Canada in giving what he called this unfavourable and mistaken verdict upon this point was the appeal to racial passions and so on. I think the hon. member completely misjudges the people of this country if he puts them down as such fools that, after a campaign of education of months and months, the vast majority of them could come to a decision dnly through appeals to passions. The people of my province came to a decision for various reasons. So far as the industry in which I was engaged is concerned, they came to that decision because they were absolutely convinced that a policy of free trade as regards the fruit growing industry would have meant the absolute extinction of, or at all events, a serious blow to that industry, in which millions of dollars were invested. Over and above that there was a very ' strong and healthy sentiment amongst the people of Canada at that time that helped to defeat the reciprocity proposal. They believed then-and I believe they do now,-that it was better, whatever 
mistakes we might make, to be master in our own house, to have complete autonomy and power and control over our own affairs, than to allow our powerful neighbour to have a finger in the pie so that in years to come she could exert over our affairs a control that might be disastrous. I do not wish to argue that point. The leader of the Opposition argued that this was not a want of confidence motion. I will recall to him what the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) said the other night.	That hon. member
said that he did not wish to see an election precipitated in this country at the present time; that he was prepared to vote against any want of confidence motion, because he did not feel it was in the interest of Canada to have an appeal to the electorate at present. My hon. friend hardly did himself justice in his taunt that our desire not to accept this amendment was because we wanted to hang on to power. I do not think my hon. friend, if he would give a conscientious expression of his opinion, will accuse any minister who has gone through the stress and strain of the last four years of being anxious and keen to hang on to power with all the nerve ranking responsibility that is entailed on members of the Government. I can only assure him for myself-and I think I can say the same thing for other members of the Government-that there have been many times when we would have gladly relinquished to others the responsibilities of power and all it entails, and I think it was rather unworthy for my hon. friend to throw out a taunt of that kind. If he thinks the desire of the Government is to hang on to power, then it is still more unworthy of him to show such an anxiety and eagerness to attain to power by the manner he proposed to the House to-night by putting an amendment of this kind. I do not agree with him when he argues that the people will realize that our position is based on a technicality. I do not think my hon. friend need think that the people of this country are so foolish as not to see through the insincerity of such an amendment at this time and not to see that it is simply a political game. We have all played it more or less in the past. There is hardly a member of this House who has not, in some form or another, been guilty of precipitating a vote, or putting the other'party on record, knowing that nothing will come of it but thinking: Here is some good ammunition I can fire out to my constitu-

ents to show what a lot of blighters these fellows were voting against the best interests of the country, at the same time knowing it was not going to be effectual.
He knows perfectly well this motion will not carry, and I venture to say the leader of the Opposition would be the most disappointed man in this House if the motion did carry and he found himself in the extraordinarily difficult position of having to form a government in this country at this time on a platform along the lines of this amendment. Plunged into the enormous tasks facing this country at the present timfi, how long would he hang on to power under these conditions? He would not last five minutes; that is my opinion.
My hon. friend from Victoria, Alta. (Mr. W. H. White) dealt at some length with our good friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark). I do not think I or any other man in this House need take up the cudgels for the hon. member for Red Deer, because I have never seen a man better able to handle them than he is himself. But I submit that there was absolutely no argument whatever in taunting the hon. member for Red Deer for voting on a motion on May 29, 1917, of a fiscal character, at a time when the Budget was six weeks old. We all know how ardently the hon. member for Red Deer has advocated the cause of free trade, but I venture to say that even if he had been on that side of the House he would not have voted for this amendment, or would have done his best not to have it introduced at such a time if the Budget had been coming down on May 29 and the amendment had been moved on April 24, because he would have known perfectly well what it would have involved. His position was absolutely consistent.
There is sometimes an approach to hypocrisy in this House in regard to political and tariff matters. I think if we told the absolute truth we should express the conviction that the tariff is in a very large measure a local matter. I know that in British Columbia we are mostly protectionists. Speaking for my constituents, they are protectionists because it is a matter of life and death with them in their industries. Coming to the prairies-I am not criticising at all-farming is carried on under different conditions, and the farmers there believe that free trade will in the end be better for them from a financial standpoint. Coming east, the same differences exist, and it is quite natural that even in our own Unionist party on this side of the House there should be difference of opinion amongst our members. We honestly recog-53}
nize that difference do exist; there-must be honest differences honestly held, and the task of statesmanship, at all events, is in the face of extraordinary national difficulties to try to reconcile these differences to some extent. No man on earth can satisfy the (extremists of either sides. People talk about compromise. It reminds me of thie old story that was told of a man and his wife who had a violent quarrel over what colour they should paint their house. The man stuck to it that it should be painted greten. The wife insisted it should be painted white. A friend later asked the husband how the matter ended, and he replied:	"We effected a compromise."
" What colour did you paint the house eventually?" The husband said:	"We
compromised on white."' That was the wife's idea of a compromise, and I think lots of people would like a compromise along those lines. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition who is so wild in his enthusiasm for the amendment of his friend from Brom'e, and who possibly, whilst he is in Opposition, would support my hon. friend who has just sat down, who declared for absolute free tracte, has never shown any keen enthusiasm for free trade, and he will probably not get up in his place and say he is in favour of fre-e iron or free coal, because hie knows perfectly well that these things affect different parts of the country differently. If he wishes to say that.he is in favour of free iron or free coal now is the tirn-e, as my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) would say, to state so. Now what is the good of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition.saying: " We deal openly and above board?" And he talks about toon, members on this side of the House rushing to get into line when the party whip is cracked. I have a high personal regard for my hon. friend, but I must say that, politically, I hava*. never seen in this House a more slavish adherent to the party whip and the party system than the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition. Again and again, during the last ten years,
I have known my hon. friend get up ancl vote against amendments of this kind on going into Supply, not on vital questions which would overturn the fiscal system of the country, but on matters of an entirely trivial character,	and
that had	no bearing on	the
substantial policies of the Government. Again and again I have known him get up w and vote against such an amendment on going into Supply, on the ground that it was a vote of want of confidence. Let me say to hon. gentlemen opposite that amend-

mehts of this kind, and much of the discussion to which I have listened thus far since the House met, show too feverish an anxiety to try and break the affiliations which at all events hold now various members on this side of the House, who have perhaps thoroughly strong antagonisms or honest differences of opinions on trade matters. There is too feverish an anxiety to try and split up the members on this side of the House who have come here for a high and noble purpose, and who naturally do not want to split up so long as the present conditions face the .world. I would say to my Unionist associates-and I am speaking as an old-time member of the Conservative party and of the Conservative Government-I admire the men who came into Union Government because (and I say this advisedly) they showed a far higher sense of proportion than hon. gentlemen opposite. They showed a real knowledge of values; they knew something of the differences between essentials and non-essentials. They left political friends and joined political opponents, than which there is, perhaps, no more distasteful task to any man in public life. Thdy joined political opponents whom they had berated and with whom they had perhaps had very acrimonious discussions in this House. They turned from policies which they had advocated vigorously, simply because they realized they were small in comparison with the infinitely greater matters facing the nation at that time. My hon. friend from. Red iDeer was one of these men, and I especially admire him for this reason: there was no man on that side of the House who had advocated so vigorously and so consistently the policy of free trade; I venture to say that he was the only member I have seen on that side of the House during the time I have been a member since 1908 who has unceasingly and consistently preached the same gospel in regard to fiscal matters. I admire him for realizing that these things were as nothing in the balance against the pressing and deadly danger that faced this nation at that time. I say it is infinitely to his honour and the honour of other hon. members who did the same thing that the non-essentials counted_ as nothing against the pressing, grievous' and deadly danger facing this country in 1917 and 1918. Talk about taxation and differences of opinion as to taxation methods. What would these have mattered if that danger had become an actuality? If the Hun had won we should have sweated under the most grievous kind of direct and indirect taxation for a lifetime. These men knew that, and not only 
to my mind did they take the right stand, but they took the sound view according to the opinion of those like the hon. member for Skeena (Lt.-Col. Peck), who pointed out the other day that those who were in the trenches fighting that bloody fight for freedom knew that was the right course if the Empire was to be saved.
Those hon. gentlemen who came over and joined us are now taunted because they happened formerly to have held certain trade theories and convictions, and hon. members op the other side seek to embarrass tjiem and the Government by a resolution which they know they cannot carry, and do not want to carry, but which they propose simply to put those who have joined the Government in an invidious position in the House and before the country. I do not think that the people of this country are so foolish as my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition assumes they are. I do not belong to the same political school as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), although we were born in the same country and lived there for many years. I belong to an opposite school of political thought; but as I look across the seas at this juncture of the world's history, perhaps more grave and portentous than at any period during the war-at all events equally so-with all the terrific turmoil and confusion, military, political, social, ethnological, and fiscal; untest in every phase of life,-as I look across the seas and consider this state of affairs, I feel that our older theories of life are upset and that there is no man either over there or in Canada who can say at the present moment exactly what political doctrine should be preached and what line of policy should be laid down. My hon. friend from Red Deer was of the same political faith as Mr. Lloyd George- a school of thought that I as a Conservative was brohght up to detest, and I would like to call the attention of the House to the fact that Mr. Lloyd George, an ardent exponent of advanced Liberalism, during the war, sat side by side with many dyed-in-the-wool political opponents, and indeed is still so sitting to-day because he sees that party affiliations are of smaller moment than the great issues that should make for national and international unity.
The country will not mistake the attitude of the House in a Vote on a question of this kind at the present time. They know that there are greater things than putting into effect or rejecting this particular piece of political economy. They know that there are greater and vastly more important things that must be done in the face of the dangers threatening the whole

world; and that it is absolutely essential, if the world is to be saved from the greatest of all evils-which my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) seemed the other day to hold rather lightly, the peril of Bolshevism,-if we are to hold the sanity of this world and preserve it against the inroads of what all thoughtful men regard as the gravest menace with which we are faced, graver perhaps than even the war; they know that there must be on the part of thoughtful men a recognition of what things are great and what are not great but merely temporary. And it seems to me that the salvation of this country, as of other countries, lies in the frank recognition of differences, and the full determination to reconcile, in the face of bigger things, these differences, and the determination above all things that we shall not be pushed aside from our path by little catch votes but shall recognize that there are larger purposes in view which we intend to achieve.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity a few days ago, in a recent debate, of expressing my views on the general tariff question, and therefore I do not deem it necessary that I should enlarge upon them now. I am reluctant to give a silent vote on this matter, the more so because I am obliged to differ from the hon. gentlemen who sit on your left, and with whom, I assure you, I am more anxious to agree than to disagree. I do not agree with all that was said by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) in his opposition to this resolution. I cannot at all concur in the opinion he expressed that any motion in amendment to Supply is necessarily a vote of want of confidence, though this particular one may be argued to be such. A motion in Supply is one of the occasions on which the representatives of the people have an opportunity to present their grievances, if they have any. It is an opportunity for free discussion, and it is not an unusual thing to have an amendment to Supply moved. My hon. friend drew a distressful picture of what would happen if the amendment to Supply carried. Why do we go into Supply? He says it is to vote money for railways, public works, soldiers, and pensions; and that all this would be stopped if anybody moved an amendment to Supply. That is altogether a mistaken notion. The parliamentary rule was read by the leader of the Opposition, but I know from my own experience that
again and again motions in amendment to Supply have been accepted. I have not turned up the records, but I have no doubt it can be found that more than once, when I was Minister of Finance, I accepted motions of that character. Nor do I agree with my friend when he says that we should wait until the Peace Conference deals with our tariff matters. If he will not deem it offensive, I must describe this as some of the "eye-wash" we get concerning Canada and the conference. There is no fiscal question concerning Canada before the Peace Conference. Tlie fiscal questions of Canada must be settled here on the floor of this Parliament. Our right to settle them is beyond dispute, and we will not surrender it to Downing Street or the War Cabinet; neither will we surrender it to the Peace Conference or the League of Nations. We retain that right, and need not wait a single moment to see what the Peace Conference intends to do regarding the matter.
I have not had the opportunity of studying the motion that has been read by way of amendment, but from its general tenor I know it is in accordance, largely, possibly wholly, with my owti views upon the tariff questions which are more or less agitating the country. It may be asked, "If the motion is in accordance with your views, why not support it?" Well, I agree with the Minister of Finance that the motion is not opportune at this time. I am obliged to take that position for several reasons. If I were younger and more enthusiastic, less experienced and less responsible, I might feel free to vote for the motion. But I happen to have been Minister of Finance for a period of fifteen years-longer, I am informed, than any other man. Therefore I know something about how tariff questions have been dealt with in Parliament, and I look back on my own experience and put myself for a moment in the position of the Finance Minister. It is well, in considering public questions, sometimes to place yourself in the opposite position. And I ask myself the question, if I were Minister of Finance to-day how would I view this motion. I have to view it as I viewed similar motions when I was Minister of Finance. The records, I am sure, will show that on several occasions, at an early stage of the session, efforts were made to commit the House to particular actions in tariff matters, and I argued that it was appropriate to wait until the Budget was under consideration. If I took that view when I was Minister of Finance, why should I change it today merely because another hon. gentleman

happens to be occupying that position? I do not think this is the right moment for raising the question. It is a fair case of applying the rule to do unto others as one would have done to him. If I were Minister of Finance to-day I should have to regard this motion as inopportune, and that being the case, I regret very much that I cannot join my hon. friends on your left in supporting it. Later on the question will come up again, but for the present I do not think the motion is a wise one, and it should not prevail.
Mr. FRANCIS N. McCREA (Sherbrooke): Mr. Speaker, before casting my vote on this amendment I wish to explain my position. The amendment contains much that I approve of, but there are some features in it which do not meet with my approval. I deem these to be unjust, and consequently I shall be compelled to vote against the amendment.	*
Doubtless I am looked upon as a manufacturer, and that designation is correct, but I wish to place the House in possession of the facts with respect to my attitude in the tariff. In the products that my firm turns out we are prepared to meet the competition of the world; we need no protection, and would be only too glad if free trade were to prevail. What we produce we sell in the open market and are prepared to meet the competition of the world-in fact we invite that competition. On the other hand, very much of the materials that enter into the manufacture of our goods and the construction of our plant are subject to a high duty. Speaking for myself personally, and as one engaged in manufacturing operations, free trade would be welcomed in our business. But I recognize there are some industries that do not occupy such a position, and that are not prepared to compete against the world. That is my position as a manufacturer speaking on this question.
This afternoon while the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) was explaining his amendment, and the Finance Minister was replying, I was absent from the Chamber. I understand, however, that the latter hon. gentleman said I looked very uncomfortable, and that he did not think I was enjoying the situation. I may have looked uncomfortable, but I was thinking of the unjust features embodied in the amendment submitted by the hon. member, for Brome.

Hear, hear.
Mr. MoCREA: Hon. gentlemen had better hesitate a moment before they applaud.

That brought to my mind the unjust treatment which our industry has received. I do not wish to be offensive to the Finance Minister, but it recalled the unfair and unjust treatment that the industry with which I am connected has suffered at the hands of the Government, and that, no doubt, accounted for my doleful look.
The hon. member for Prince, P.E.I., (Mr. J. Read) in his speech to-night declared in very emphatic terms that the public press of Canada had been debauched-had been bribed, bought, and paid for and so on- with the people's money. I am inclined to think the hon. gentleman is not in possession of all the facts upon which he based his statement. I am not, and therefore I cannot say how much public money went to paying, or buying the public press; but I do wish to say that about a million and a half of the newsprint manufacturers' money was devoted towards buying the press of Canada in the last election, and since that time. That is to say, the manufacturers of newsprint in Canada during the last two years have had to contribute the necessary paper for the press of Canada at about a million and a half of dollars less than they would have received if they had been allowed to sell newsprint in the open market of the United States and elsewhere. Consequently I say that is what it has cost the manufacturers of newsprint in Canada to support the Government. We have heard the emphatic statement from hon. gentlemen on both sides that they do not want an election at the present time. Certainly from the paper manufacturers' standpoint we do not want an election just now if we have to pay the newspapers the same price we paid last election.
In part the amendment does meet with my entire approval. That is in so far as it calls for the acceptance of reciprocity as specified and laid down in the agreement of 1911. I was in favour of reciprocity at that time, and for that reason presented myself as a candidate in the county of Sherbrooke where I succeeded in being elected, although that county had never previously returned a Liberal member.
The features of the amendment to which I object, and which I say are unjust and unfair, especially at this particular time, are those which are likely to make inroads into our revenue. Faced, as we are now, with an enormous debt, when the expenditures of the country call for $437,000,000- and I venture to say that when the supplementary Estimates are brought down the total will be swollen to approximately half a billion of dollars-the situation calls for the exercise of caution. If every man is

to be exempt from paying his fair share of taxation, if all are not to be required to contribute towards the revenue, where is the money coming from to meet our national necessities? That is the question that puzzles me. If we did not require money on this vast scale I would be a free trader, but on a- basis in which all parties would be placed on a position of equality. The amendment calls for the placing of agricultural implements of all kinds, and mill and mining machinery, on the free list, but other industries are to remain untouched. Let me give an illustration of what the effect of this will be. Supposing there is in the city of Ottawa a large manufacturer of farm implements, and on the . other side of the street there is a manufacturer who produces another class of goods on an extensive scale. Both men import a great part of the raw material whidh enters into the manufacture of their products. The man who manufactures farm implements is allowed to import his steel, iron, and brass, the metals of all kinds which he needs, his paint and other materials, free of duty. The man on the other side of the street has to pay a duty on his raw articles, and has to compete in the labour market, has to pay the same wages, and meet other outlays on the same scale. Where is the fairness in that kind of tariff arrangement? If it is possible to reduce the tariff let us do so, but let that reduction be carried out on a uniform basis, and not select certain industries for favoured treatment.
It would appear that the population in the western provinces are largely farmers, and they represent a great many votes. Is it the interest of the country we are supposed to be working for, or are we influenced by the desire to gain the votes of these farmers? For my part, I believe the present to be too serious a time to play politics; it is too serious a time to be bidding for votes. I do not believe in a tariff when it reaches the point that it protects industries in this country; then it is too high. But I do say that the manufacturers of this country with its population of some seven and a half million people are not in a position to compete with the manufacturers of England or the United States, and they must have some protection as tariff for revenue. There is no man more anxious to help the farmers than I am, hut there are two sides to the farmers' question. If you give the farmers free implements and everything else, and if they have no population to sell their crops to, what are they going to do
with them? I say that it is just as essential that we should build up industries in this country and create centres to consume the products of the farm as it is for the farmers to produce, and the way to do that, in my judgment, is for this Government and for the people of this country to work out some policy which will be fair and reasonable and equitable to all parties-a tariff to produce revenue. I do not think it makes very much difference whether we call upon the farmers of the West to put their hands down into their pockets and pay direct taxes or call upon them to pay in the shape of a duty on implements, provided that that duty does not build up a tariff wall and enable the manufacturers to put the money in their pockets.
I he manufacturers of this country, in my judgment, must have some protection, and if I may be allowed, Mr. Speaicer, I wish to take up a little of the time of the House to illustrate just what I mean. I have never had anything to do with any branch of business except the one I am engaged in, but I have had a little insight into this one particular line of business. A man with whom I was connected for some ten years and very familiar with was a shoemaker, as were his father and grandfather before him. This man had two factories employing about twenty-five hundred people and manufactured four or five different grades of boots, common men's and boys' boots. The boot from when it started with the	side of	leather	until it	reachedthe	finished	article	probably	passed	.
t through the hands of twenty-five or thirty men, and every man had to do his share . of that work down to the twentieth part of a cent. The man who cut the leather had to furnish so many taps, so many soles and so many heels out of each piece of leather; if he did not he had to give an explanation to the foreman. The outcome of that was that they got this particular business down to a science. The man who owned this shop and showed me through it several times, told me that when they made five cents a pair net profit they were doing good business and able to pay substantial dividends. Why? Because they had a population of 110,000,000 people to sell to and could specialize. Now our boot and shoe manufacturers, with our population of 7,000,000, have to make everything from the finest lady's shoe to the brogan, and cannot specialize on anything, and that applies to every other branch of business. We are

not in a position to compete with the old-established concerns which have had this experience, specializing in every branch and favoured with a large home market; and until we reach that point it would be folly to throw down the tariff wall entirely.
I	understand that the majority on both sides of the House are not in favour of throwing down the tariff wall. But why
throw it down on certain articles
II	p.m. and not on others? As I explained at the outset, the reason I am opposed to this is because of the injustice of removing the tariff from certain things and leaving it on others. That is too long a jump to start off with. If it is possible to reduce the tariff generally, let us do it. Tariff for revenue is all we need, and I think that the common sense and wisdom of the people of this country, both in the West and everywhere else, will force them to the conclusion that as members of a portion of this Empire and responsible for the debts of this country, it is their duty to contribute their fair share, and they may as well do it in the form of revenue as by the way of direct taxation.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak on this question, but I find the discussion is so interesting that I feel I ought to express my views on the subject before the House.
I am not a manufacturer nor interested in the manufactures of any commodities, but I represent a thriving constituency within the city of Montreal in w.hich there are quite a number of manufacturing industries. I tell you honestly, Sir, that I be-, lieve it is my duty as representative of that constituency to vote against the amendment, and I shall do so. First, because I believe that this is not an opportune time to bring forward an amendment of this character. .Second, because I am going to put before this House the business reasons why I believe -nat I should vote against it. I have just received a resolution from the Board of Trade of Montreal, which represents the trade interests of the city and knows something aoout tariffs and questions of commerce-
They did not vote for you.

I do not care. I have confidence in their reasons and I believe in them. I quite agree with their views on this matter.

This resolution which I have received from the Montreal Board of Trade is dated March 21, 1919:

I rise to a point of
order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member has no right to -address himself to me directly; his protest must go through you, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for St. James has the floor and I hope he will not be interrupted again.

I will continue my reading of the Montreal Board of Trade resolution:
Whereas, at this time when our fighting forces are returning from overseas in large numbers and they, together with munition workers, are seeking other employment, business must be stimulated to create confidence and stability in commercial enterprises, thereby providing for the maximum employment of labour,-
Whereas, values of all commodities are in process of re-adjustment, and any changes in the present fiscal policy would tend to delay the return to normal conditions, retard initiative and create uncertainty,-
Whereas, because of the heavy adverse balance of trade as between Canada and the United States, as evidenced by the continued high premium oi ever 2 per cent for the .purchase of New York funds, importations from the United States should be kept at a minimum, more especially of such commodities as are made in Canada or as are non-essential,-
Whereas, Great Britain, France and other European countries have seen fit to restrict imports and thereby conserve their own resources and provide employment for their own people,- Whereas, the burden of taxation must be borne by all classes, and not be sectional, it is therefore necessary that all classes, including farmers, manufacturers, merchants and workers should be fully employed, and thereby make Canada more than ever self contained and less reliant upon imports from other countries,- Therefore resolved.-That the Council of the Montreal Board of Trade is of the opinion that until a definite tariff policy is adopted for the British Empire, the Dominion Government should exercise, during the period of reconstruction, some degree of special control over all imports, either by a license system or otherwise.

The Chainbre de Commerc'e of Montreal, which*, includes many able business men and manufacturers, will certainly, at the proper time, pass resolutions similar to this. I have not yet recieved any, but I expect some, because some of my friends who belong to that organization-manufacturers of shoes, leathers and so on-are not specially in favour of too much free trade to-day. There was some difficulty in getting some of the manufacturers in my county to understand they should vote Liberal at the ,1911 election; many of them voted for me from a personal standpoint. But some of them were afraid of their trade at that time. I am taking this position, reserving, of cours'e, the right to Whatever opinion I consider proper when the Government brings down its tariff proposals.
I was paired with the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden). Had I voted I would have voted for the amendment.
I was paired with the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton). Had I voted, I would have voted for the amendment.

Motion (Sir Thomas White) agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply,-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The present fiscal year ends on the 31st of the present month. I have spoken with the leader of the Opposition (Mr. D. D. McKenzie) with a view of obtaining, as is usual, an interim supply of two months. With his concurrence, I desire to move:
Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $52,310,026.12 being one-sixth of the amount of each item set forth in the Main Estimates for the year ending 31st March, 1920, laid on the Table of the House on the 19th instant, be granted to His Majesty for the year ending 31st March, 1920.
Did I understand the Acting Prime Minister to say "with the consent of the leader of the Opposition," or "with the consent of the House."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated "with the concurrence of the leader of the Opposition," and I assumed that the other members would also concur.
I just wished to know whether there were any other members in the House than the two leaders.

What the leader of the Government says, namely, that so far as he and myself can concur in this resolution, we have done so, is quite true, but, of course, that was with the expectation that the House would concur. I wish nevertheless to reserve certain rights which the members of the Opposition have in connection with all the items as they come up for consideration later on. Rule 17 (c) of the Rules of the House reads:
On Thursday's and Fridays when the Order of the Hay is called for the House to go into Committee of Supply, or of Ways and Means, M,r. Speaker shall leave the Chair without putting any question, provided that, except by the consent of the House, the Estimates of each department shall be first taken uip on a day other than Thursday or Friday.

It might be argued later on that all the items were taken up on this resolution, and that consequently this rule did not apply. I want to reserve the right that this rule will be regarded as in force in connection with the Estimates of any department that may come up, notwithstanding that we are consenting by this resolution to one-sixth of the Estimates of all the departments being passed, and also to reserve to ourselves, or to any member who may so desire, the right to criticise any particular item of the Estimates of any department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend's request is entirely reasonable and I have much pleasure in agreeing to it.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time, and concurred in.
On motion of Sir Thomas White (Acting Prime Minister) the House went into Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
